questions.prompt: Why might cosine similarity produce poor retrieval even with a strong embedding model?
questions.referenceAnswer: A strong embedding model does not fix the retrieval pipeline. Poor chunking can separate answers from their context. Queries and documents may use incompatible formats or domains; normalization and index distance settings must agree. Similarity thresholds may discard relevant evidence. Semantic similarity is not the same as task relevance, so evaluate hybrid retrieval and reranking on labeled queries.
keyPoints: Poor document chunking
Query/document mismatch
Embedding normalization issues
Domain mismatch
Similarity threshold problems
Semantic similarity is not relevance
Hybrid retrieval or reranking

questions.prompt: How would you determine the optimal chunk size experimentally?
questions.referenceAnswer: Create a labeled query set and hold the embedding model, corpus and retrieval budget fixed. Compare chunk sizes and overlap settings, measure recall and ranking quality, and evaluate downstream answer faithfulness, latency and cost. Keep a held-out split to check that the chosen size generalizes.
keyPoints: Labeled query set and held-out split
Vary chunk size and overlap
Control other pipeline settings
Measure retrieval and answer quality
Measure latency and cost

questions.prompt: Your retrieval recall is high, but final answer quality is poor. Where would you investigate next?
questions.referenceAnswer: Inspect whether the relevant passage reaches the final prompt after reranking, truncation and context packing. Check distracting evidence, conflicting sources and citation instructions. Evaluate grounding and answer correctness separately from retrieval recall, and inspect generation settings and model limitations.
keyPoints: Reranking and context packing
Truncation or distracting evidence
Conflicting sources and citation instructions
Grounding versus retrieval recall
Generation settings and model limitations

questions.prompt: What does RAG add to the generation process that a plain LLM call doesn't have?
questions.referenceAnswer:
Answer: Relevant passages retrieved from an external knowledge source, inserted into the prompt so generation is grounded in that specific retrieved material

RAG's defining feature is retrieval: pulling in relevant external content and conditioning generation on it, rather than relying purely on what the model happened to learn during training.
keyPoints: RAG's defining feature is retrieval: pulling in relevant external content and conditioning generation on it, rather than relying purely on what the model happened to learn during training.

questions.prompt: Why doesn't a very large context window make retrieval-based approaches unnecessary?
questions.referenceAnswer:
Answer: Sending a huge amount of context on every query is expensive and slow, and the 'lost in the middle' effect means the model doesn't reliably attend to everything even when it technically fits

Even a technically large-enough context window doesn't solve the cost, latency, and reliable-attention problems — retrieval's job of surfacing only what's actually relevant remains valuable regardless of how much a model's context window can theoretically hold.
keyPoints: Even a technically large-enough context window doesn't solve the cost, latency, and reliable-attention problems — retrieval's job of surfacing only what's actually relevant remains valuable regardless of how much a model's context window can theoretically hold.

questions.prompt: What information should typically be stored alongside each chunk's embedding in a RAG knowledge base?
questions.referenceAnswer:
Answer: Metadata like the source document, section or page, last-updated date, and access-control information, which enables filtering and accurate citation later

Storing metadata alongside each embedding is what enables the metadata filtering and citation capabilities a real RAG system needs — treating it as an essential part of the index rather than an optional add-on.
keyPoints: Storing metadata alongside each embedding is what enables the metadata filtering and citation capabilities a real RAG system needs — treating it as an essential part of the index rather than an optional add-on.

questions.prompt: What is the key structural difference between embedding-based retrieval and a cross-encoder reranker?
questions.referenceAnswer:
Answer: Embedding-based retrieval encodes the query and each document separately and compares vectors, while a cross-encoder feeds the query and a candidate document together into one model, letting them interact directly during scoring

The fundamental difference is separate versus joint encoding: embeddings compare independently-computed vectors (fast, scalable), while a cross-encoder processes the query and document together, allowing much richer interaction at the cost of being far more computationally expensive.
keyPoints: The fundamental difference is separate versus joint encoding: embeddings compare independently-computed vectors (fast, scalable), while a cross-encoder processes the query and document together, allowing much richer interaction at the cost of being far more computationally expensive.

questions.prompt: What does a well-assembled RAG prompt typically include beyond just the raw retrieved text?
questions.referenceAnswer: Effective RAG prompt assembly structures the retrieved material clearly — labeled, separated sources plus explicit instructions — rather than just pasting chunks together with no organization.
keyPoints: Effective RAG prompt assembly structures the retrieved material clearly — labeled, separated sources plus explicit instructions — rather than just pasting chunks together with no organization.

choices.text: Nothing more is needed; raw concatenated text is always sufficient
Clear separation between chunks, a label or reference number per chunk to support citation, and a system-level instruction on exactly how to use the provided context
Only the user's original question, with no context included at all
A complete copy of the entire knowledge base, not just the retrieved chunks

questions.prompt: How can a RAG system detect that retrieval genuinely didn't find good matches for a query?
questions.referenceAnswer: Using the calibrated similarity threshold approach from the embeddings course, consistently low scores across retrieved candidates is a concrete, detectable signal that the knowledge base likely doesn't actually cover the query well.
keyPoints: Using the calibrated similarity threshold approach from the embeddings course, consistently low scores across retrieved candidates is a concrete, detectable signal that the knowledge base likely doesn't actually cover the query well.

choices.text: This situation is impossible to detect and can only be discovered by the user reporting a bad answer

By checking similarity scores across all retrieved candidates against a calibrated threshold (from the embeddings course) — consistently low scores signal that retrieval likely didn't find genuinely relevant content
Retrieval always finds a good match for every possible query with no exceptions
Only by manually reviewing every single query after the fact

questions.prompt: What makes RAG 'agentic' compared to standard, fixed-pipeline RAG?
questions.referenceAnswer: The defining feature is giving the model agency over retrieval itself — using the tool-calling mechanism to let it decide when, whether, and how to search, rather than forcing every query through an identical fixed pipeline.
keyPoints: The defining feature is giving the model agency over retrieval itself — using the tool-calling mechanism to let it decide when, whether, and how to search, rather than forcing every query through an identical fixed pipeline.

choices.text: Agentic RAG always uses a completely different embedding model than standard RAG

Retrieval is exposed as a tool the model can choose to call, deciding for itself whether retrieval is needed, what to search for, and whether to search again, rather than always running the same fixed retrieval step
Agentic RAG never actually performs any retrieval at all
There is no meaningful difference between agentic and standard RAG

questions.prompt: What does a RAG-specific eval set need beyond a general LLM application eval set's question-answer pairs?
questions.referenceAnswer: Including expected source documents alongside each question-answer pair is what makes it possible to separately measure context precision/recall (retrieval quality) from faithfulness (generation quality), rather than only getting an aggregate end-to-end score.
keyPoints: Including expected source documents alongside each question-answer pair is what makes it possible to separately measure context precision/recall (retrieval quality) from faithfulness (generation quality), rather than only getting an aggregate end-to-end score.

choices.text: Nothing additional; a general eval set is always sufficient for RAG systems too
The specific source document(s) that should actually be retrieved to support each expected answer, which enables measuring retrieval quality separately from generation quality
Only the exact wording the model must use, with no flexibility
A complete copy of the entire knowledge base for every example

questions.prompt: RAG latency increases from 800 ms to 4 seconds. What would you inspect first, and why?
questions.referenceAnswer: Trace retrieval, reranking and generation separately. Inspect candidate count, context length and queue time. Compare latency percentiles under the same workload before and after the change.
keyPoints: Trace retrieval, reranking and generation separately.
Inspect candidate count, context length and queue time.
Compare latency percentiles under the same workload before and after the change.

questions.prompt: How would you test that the change fixed this incident rather than hiding it?
questions.referenceAnswer: Keep a reproducible failing case for this incident. Compare latency percentiles under the same workload before and after the change. Compare the same workload before and after the change; record both the target metric and regressions.
keyPoints: Compare latency percentiles under the same workload before and after the change.
Compare the same workload before and after the change.
Check regressions as well as the target metric.

questions.prompt: The fix works in a small test but fails at production scale. What next?

Measure a representative workload.

questions.prompt: Which components belong in a tenant-isolated enterprise RAG design? Select all that apply.
questions.referenceAnswer: Enforce identity at the gateway, permissions during retrieval, and isolation in caches. A model instruction cannot replace application authorization. A semantically similar question from another tenant does not authorize reuse of private evidence.
keyPoints: Authenticated tenant identity
Permission-aware retrieval
Tenant-scoped caches
Authorization outside the model

choices.text: An authenticated gateway that supplies tenant identity
Retrieval that enforces document access permissions
Caches scoped by tenant, model version and relevant context
A shared answer cache keyed only by semantic similarity
A model prompt as the only authorization check

questions.prompt: Order the stages of this RAG pipeline, from document ingestion to a grounded answer.
questions.referenceAnswer: Ingest source documents → Split documents into chunks → Create chunk embeddings → Store embeddings and metadata → Retrieve candidates for the query → Rerank retrieved candidates → Assemble the grounded prompt → Generate an answer with citations. Ingestion and indexing happen before query-time retrieval. Reranking refines candidates before context assembly and generation.
